text: Lesson twenty-three loaded a model and got back raw numbers, not an answer. Getting from there to something useful has two paths: trust an existing fine-tune, or train the model further yourself. This lesson is how to tell which one you need.

Using as-is means calling a model someone already fine-tuned for your exact task, with no training of your own. Lesson twenty-three's sentiment pipeline was exactly this — already trained on a large labeled dataset for general English sentiment. Fine-tuning it again on a tiny dataset of your own would likely make it worse.

Fine-tuning takes the pretrained weights as a starting point instead of random ones, then keeps training with the same backpropagation from chapter four, on your own labeled data. In code: load the model, set training arguments, hand both to a trainer, and call train.

Two details matter. The model already knows general language going in. And the learning rate is deliberately tiny — two times ten to the negative five here, against the point five a toy network used in lesson nineteen — so training nudges the weights toward your task without wiping out what they already know. That failure mode has a name: catastrophic forgetting.

This is a real TensorBoard dashboard, hosted directly on a Hugging Face model repository's training metrics tab — actual loss and gradient-norm charts from a real training run, the same kind of signal lesson nineteen's tiny loss curve showed, just at a much larger scale.

Because a fine-tune starts from a specific base model, the Hub tracks that lineage directly. This real model card shows "Finetuned from mistralai slash Mistral seven B," with a link to view the base model or list every other model finetuned from it — a fast way to check whether someone already did your fine-tune for you.

A Hub repository is a git repository underneath, so even a small model card edit is a diffable, attributed commit — this is a real one. Fine-tuning produces exactly this kind of auditable change when you push the result, not an untracked swap of files.

Use as-is when an existing fine-tune already fits; fine-tune when your domain or task doesn't match what's already out there. Next lesson looks at the bigger idea underneath this whole chapter: transfer learning, and why starting from a pretrained model works at all.
